summary: Specifies the prospero URI scheme, originally defined in RFC 1738. It was written so RFC 1738 could be made obsolete while keeping information about the scheme on record. This document is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4157 records how a prospero URI identifies a resource through the Prospero Directory Service. The RFC is Historic and notes that Prospero was not widely implemented and almost no servers were in use at the time.

questions: what is the prospero uri scheme
what does a prospero uri identify
subtitle: The URI form used to locate resources through the Prospero Directory Service.

tldr.problem: The definition of the prospero URI scheme was in RFC 1738, which was being made obsolete while information about the scheme needed to be retained.
tldr.mechanism: A prospero URI identifies a host-specific object name and optional field/value pairs, which a Prospero server interprets to determine access methods.
tldr.outcome: The RFC preserves the scheme definition and notes that Prospero was not widely implemented and almost no servers were in use at publication; the unit marks it Historic.

today: The unit metadata marks RFC 4157 as Historic. The RFC notes that almost no Prospero servers were in use at the time it was written.

sections.title: Why the Scheme Was Recorded Again
sections.content:
Many URI schemes were first defined in RFC 1738. Because that document had become obsolete, RFC 4157 copies the prospero scheme definition so information about it remains available.

The prospero scheme designates resources accessed through the Prospero Directory Service. The URI points to a host-specific object name that the Prospero server interprets.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC preserves the prospero address format after its earlier source document became obsolete. The address directs a client to a Prospero directory server.

sections.title: Parts of a Prospero URI
sections.content:
A prospero URI contains a host, an optional port, and a host-specific object name. If the port is omitted, the default is 1525; usernames and passwords are not allowed in the URI.

Optional semicolon-separated field/value pairs can identify the target, such as a particular object version. The object name is opaque to the client, and slashes within it do not guarantee a hierarchical structure.
sections.plainLanguage: The URI names a server and an object that the server understands. Extra fields can narrow the target, but clients should not assume the object name has a particular structure.

sections.title: Security and Historical Context
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the Prospero protocol uses passwords in clear text for authentication and provides no privacy. It describes both properties as extremely unsafe in current practice.

The document also says that Prospero was not widely implemented and almost no Prospero servers were in use at the time of writing. The unit metadata marks this document Historic.
sections.plainLanguage: The URI scheme does not protect Prospero passwords or data. The RFC records the format for a protocol that had little deployment at the time.
